content.title: Ruling on Participating in and Giving Greetings on Non-Muslim Religious Festivals
content.subtitle: May the lights of celebration not blur the boundaries of Tawheed.
content.body:
During autumn, the continuous beat of drums and surrounding noise drift through the air. Artificial lights and the commotion around the festival mandaps create a strange atmosphere. Many consider it harmless to visit out of curiosity at a friend’s request or to admire the decorations of clay idols. We may think, “I am not offering anjali or raising my hands in worship or devotion; I have only come to look!” But have we ever stopped to think—when people deny the sovereignty of the very Lord before whom we stand in prayer at least seventeen times every day and declare, “You alone we worship,” and place His own creation on the seat of worship and pray to it, how great an act of self-deception and spiritual heedlessness can a believer’s mere presence there out of curiosity become?

The Call to Tawheed and the Uncompromising Command of Our Lord

Allah, the Lord of the worlds, has declared unequivocally in the Holy Qur’an:

“And worship Allah and associate nothing with Him...” (Surah An-Nisa, 4:36)

A believer’s greatest treasure is their Iman—faith in Tawheed and the Oneness of Allah. Bowing before a clay idol believed to remove hardship or possess power is not merely visiting a fair or admiring craftsmanship. It is participating in a ritual that places something alongside the One and Only Creator of the heavens and the earth.

The Silent Approval Behind “Shubho Sharodiya”

Many of us think, what harm could there be in saying a few pleasant words to make a non-Muslim friend or colleague happy? But the entire atmosphere of Durga Puja revolves around the arrival and worship of the goddess according to their beliefs. When a Muslim greets someone with “Shubho Sharodiya” or “Shubho Bijoya,” it indirectly expresses approval of that worship and belief. Can a believer ever say, “May your shirk be blessed,” or “May the worship of someone other than Allah be auspicious”?

Allah Himself has described shirk as the greatest injustice and declared that He may forgive any sin for whomever He wills except shirk, which He does not forgive (Surah An-Nisa, 4:48). Do we realize how much a believer’s spiritual dignity is compromised by entering such a place merely to look?

For details on the ruling regarding participation in and greetings at non-Muslims’ religious ceremonies, visit the link below:

https://muslimsday.com/blog/পূজা-দেখতে-যাওয়ার-বিধান/

The Crowd at the Mandap and the Place of Divine Wrath

Amid the incense and the sounds of bells and ritual instruments, we may not be worshipping as spectators. Yet our presence adds to the crowd and makes the display of shirk more festive. Amir al-Mu’minin Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) warned:

“Do not enter the places of worship of the polytheists on the days of their festivals, for Allah’s displeasure or wrath descends upon them.” (As-Sunan al-Kubra: 18862)

A believer’s heart cannot truly seek joy or entertainment in a place where the displeasure of their Lord descends.

Good Conduct vs. The Uncompromising Boundaries of Faith

Does this mean we should not treat non-Muslims well or stand beside them in times of hardship? Of course, we should. Islam does not teach injustice toward people of other faiths, nor does it permit insulting their objects of worship [Surah Al-An‘am, 6:108]. Ensuring their safety as fellow citizens, supporting them during illness, and showing compassion in difficult times are duties of a believer. But good social conduct and compromising one’s faith are never the same. We should neither behave rudely toward them nor wrong them in any way.

Let the glitter of celebration never conceal the true light within us. A heart illuminated by La Ilaha Illallah cannot willingly stand before an altar where clay idols are worshipped in denial of its Lord. Let us preserve the dignity and humanity of people of other faiths while protecting our own Iman with all the love in our hearts.
